# Press Release

## Fortinet Acquires Network Monitoring and Remediation Innovator Panopta

Panopta SaaS-based Hybrid Infrastructure Monitoring and Diagnostics Platform to Further Ensure Fortinet Customer Networks are High Performing and Secure Through Automated NetSec Ops

**SUNNYVALE, Calif. - Dec 9, 2020**

  
  

**Ken Xie, Founder, Chairman of the Board, and CEO**

“Given the complex and distributed nature of many IT environments, organizations need a high performance, secure network to successfully achieve their digital business initiatives. With the convergence of security and networking through a Security-driven Network approach organizations can get the connectivity and performance that is crucial to protect today’s hyper-connected businesses. Fortinet’s acquisition of Panopta complements our best-in-class security offerings with a SaaS platform that provides further network visibility and agile remediation for hybrid environments, including edge and cloud networks, to achieve even greater security and business efficiency.”

**News Summary**

[Fortinet](http://www.fortinet.com/)® (NASDAQ: FTNT), a global leader in broad, integrated and automated cybersecurity solutions, today announced it has acquired Panopta, the SaaS platform innovator that provides full stack visibility and automated management of the health of an enterprise network, including servers, network devices, containers, applications, databases, virtual appliances, and cloud infrastructure.

Customers are accelerating their digital innovation initiatives and user experience determines the success of an application. Making sure infrastructure has 100% uptime is critical. Panopta’s cloud-based solution delivers a complete picture of every service, network device, and application in any deployment, whether it is containers, cloud, on-prem, or hybrid. Fortinet’s [Security Fabric](http://www.fortinet.com/solutions/enterprise-midsize-business/security-fabric), combined with Panopta’s scalable, network monitoring and diagnostics platform, enables Fortinet to offer the most comprehensive network and security operations management solution for enterprises or service providers.

In addition to further improving customers’ hybrid network infrastructure security and performance, the combined solution is expected to enhance real-time monitoring and effectiveness of the infrastructure that powers Fortinet’s security services, including cloud-based. For instance, SASE service, email, security analytics, and web application firewalls will benefit from the continuous monitoring and diagnostics provided by Panopta’s platform. Integration between Panopta’s solution and Fortinet’s [FortiGate](http://www.fortinet.com/products/next-generation-firewall) Next-generation Firewall and [Secure SD-WAN](http://www.fortinet.com/products/sd-wan#models-specs) solution will further enhance SD-WAN connectivity and performance. Furthermore, integration of Panopta’s automated incident management with our SOAR platform can deliver a single platform view for IT teams to diagnose and resolve real-time network health incidents proactively.

Panopta’s platform is built to be partner friendly, empowering MSSPs, and value-add partners to easily integrate the multi-tenant solution into their own offering and quickly add value to their end customers. The Panopta solution’s [role-based access control](http://www.fortinet.com/resources/cyberglossary/role-based-access-control) delivers a granular governance layer between customers, and also within the Network Operations Center (NOC) and Security Operations Center (SOC) teams.

In the current remote workforce environment, the availability, performance, security, and quality of an application and its components all impact the end-user experience. Panopta’s solution analyzes both network health metrics and application performance to identify potential problem areas that may impact user access, and enables rapid, automated remediation (also called Digital Experience Monitoring or DEM).

With the Panopta acquisition, Fortinet will deliver the industry’s most comprehensive Security-driven Networking platform by adding new capabilities in network monitoring, detection and incident response. Features will include:

* Unified Monitoring and automated Incident Management that reduces response and resolution times for NOC teams and, in turn, helps exceed SLAs.
* Over 50 global points of presence (PoPS) with low-cost probes to simulate application performance and latency that may impact end user experience (also known as synthetic transaction monitoring).
* Cloud native monitoring for Kubernetes and PaaS workloads in AWS and Azure.
* Fully configurable alerting workflows with out-of-the-box integrations for third-party enterprise and modern communication tools.
* Another first-class partner-friendly service offering that remains true to Fortinet’s ongoing commitment to its valued partners.

Financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.

**Additional Resources**

* [Learn more](http://www.fortinet.com/products/fortinet-acquires-panopta) about how this acquisition strengthens Fortinet’s security portfolio and delivers the most comprehensive Security-driven Networking platform on the market. Additional insights into the acquisition can be found in this [blog](https://www.fortinet.com/blog/business-and-technology/fortinet-acquires-panopta).
* Find out how the [Fortinet Security Fabric](http://www.fortinet.com/solutions/enterprise-midsize-business/security-fabric) platform delivers broad, integrated, and automated protection across an organization’s entire digital infrastructure.
* Learn more about [FortiGuard Labs](http://www.fortinet.com/fortiguard/labs) threat intelligence and research and the [FortiGuard Security Subscriptions and Services](http://www.fortinet.com/fortiguard/labs#security-subscriptions) portfolio.
* Learn more about Fortinet’s [Network Security Expert (NSE) Training Institute](https://training.fortinet.com/ "https://training.fortinet.com/"), including its [free cybersecurity training initiative](https://www.fortinet.com/blog/business-and-technology/why-cybersecurity-training-is-more-important-than-ever.html "/content/fortinet-com/en_us/blog/business-and-technology/why-cybersecurity-training-is-more-important-than-ever.html"), the [NSE Certification Program](https://training.fortinet.com/local/staticpage/view.php?page=certifications&utm_source=pr&utm_campaign=2020-q2-nse), [Security Academy Program](https://training.fortinet.com/local/staticpage/view.php?page=fnsa) and [Veterans Program](http://www.fortinet.com/training/veterans-program "/content/fortinet-com/en_us/training/veterans-program.html").
* Read more about how [Fortinet customers](http://www.fortinet.com/customers) are securing their organizations.
* Engage in the [Fortinet User Community (Fuse)](https://fusecommunity.fortinet.com/home). Share ideas and feedback, learn more about our products and technology, and connect with peers.
* Follow Fortinet on [Twitter](https://twitter.com/Fortinet), [LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/company/fortinet), [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/fortinet/), [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/fortinet), and [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/behindthefirewall/).

### About Fortinet

Fortinet (NASDAQ: FTNT) secures the largest enterprise, service provider, and government organizations around the world. Fortinet empowers our customers with complete visibility and control across the expanding attack surface and the power to take on ever-increasing performance requirements today and into the future. Only the Fortinet Security Fabric platform can address the most critical security challenges and protect data across the entire digital infrastructure, whether in networked, application, multi-cloud or edge environments. Fortinet ranks #1 in the most security appliances shipped worldwide and more than 480,000 customers trust Fortinet to protect their businesses. Both a technology company and a learning organization, the Fortinet Network Security Expert (NSE) Training Institute has one of the largest and broadest cybersecurity training programs in the industry. Learn more at [https://www.fortinet.com](https://www.fortinet.com/), the [Fortinet Blog](https://www.fortinet.com/blog), or [FortiGuard Labs](https://www.fortinet.com/fortiguard/labs.html).

## Company Overview

Amazon Web Services Inc. (AWS) is a subsidiary of Amazon.com Inc., which provides cloud computing services. It offers a comprehensive range of cloud infrastructure services, including computing, storage, databases, networking, analytics, mobile, developer tools, augmented and virtual reality, robotics, game tech, ML, management tools, content delivery, media services, customer engagement, app streaming, and security, identity and compliance. It serves automotive, digital marketing, telecommunications, education, government, retail, financial services, media and entertainment, gaming, CPG, healthcare, life sciences, oil and gas, power, utilities, and nonprofit organizations.

AWS enables pharmaceutical companies, biotechnology firms, research institutions, and healthcare organizations to accelerate scientific discovery and innovation through its cloud-native infrastructure, HPC and AI/ML capabilities. Its offerings include platforms for genomics and multiomics analysis, clinical genomics, molecular simulations, and drug discovery workflows, supported by services such as AWS HealthOmics, AWS HPC AI/ML solutions for predictive modeling and data analytics. It has business operations in the U.S., the U.K., Australia, China, France, Germany, India, Brazil, Canada, Ireland, Japan, Korea, and Singapore.

## Insights

**Cloud Scale Opportunity** AWS's leadership in cloud infrastructure and global data center footprint positions them to scale enterprise workloads efficiently; target upsell opportunities around advanced analytics, AI/ML services, and hybrid cloud integrations to optimize cost and performance.

**Cost Optimization** The promise of variable costs and reduced capex suggests strategic opportunities to propose cost-optimization solutions, such as enterprise-grade cost management, reserved instances planning, and serverless architectures to improve margin for large-scale customers.

**Security & Compliance** As a cloud provider serving 190 countries, AWS faces diverse regulatory environments; position security posture enhancements, compliance tooling, and governance offerings to appeal to highly regulated industries seeking audit-friendly cloud solutions.

**AI and Media** Recent news on Project Lighthouse and Brand+/Performance+ updates indicate continued investment in media, streaming, and AI capabilities; explore opportunities in content delivery optimization, AI-powered recommendations, and media analytics for large media and entertainment clients.

**Expansion & Talent** New facilities and leadership hires signal ongoing growth and regional demand; approach regional enterprise accounts with localized deployments, integration services, and professional services partnerships to accelerate adoption in target markets.

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is an IT services and IT consulting company based at 410 Terry Avenue North, Duvall, Washington 98019, United States, with more than 10,000 employees. The platform enables organizations to convert capital infrastructure expenses into variable costs by accessing resources on demand, leveraging economies of scale. AWS provides a highly reliable, scalable, low-cost cloud infrastructure platform that serves hundreds of thousands of businesses in 190 countries, with data centers in the United States, Europe, Singapore, and Japan. The company operates in the IT services and IT consulting industry and offers cloud infrastructure services to customers worldwide.

# Amazon Web Services (AWS)
Official Global LinkedIn page for Amazon Web Services (AWS).
IT Services and IT Consulting • Seattle, WA • 11,015,061 followers • 10,001+ employees

## Overview
Launched in 2006, Amazon Web Services (AWS) began exposing key infrastructure services to businesses in the form of web services -- now widely known as cloud computing. The ultimate benefit of cloud computing, and AWS, is the ability to leverage a new business model and turn capital infrastructure expenses into variable costs. Businesses no longer need to plan and procure servers and other IT resources weeks or months in advance. Using AWS, businesses can take advantage of Amazon's expertise and economies of scale to access resources when their business needs them, delivering results faster and at a lower cost. Today, Amazon Web Services provides a highly reliable, scalable, low-cost infrastructure platform in the cloud that powers hundreds of thousands of businesses in 190 countries around the world. With data center locations in the U.S., Europe, Singapore, and Japan, customers across all industries are taking advantage of our low cost, elastic, open and flexible, secure platform.

**Amazon Web Services, Inc.** (**AWS**) is a subsidiary of [Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_(company) "Amazon (company)") that provides [on-demand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_as_a_service "Software as a service") [cloud computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing") [platforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computing_platform "Computing platform") and [APIs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/API "API") to individuals, companies, and governments, on a metered, pay-as-you-go basis.

Clients often use this in combination with [autoscaling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elasticity_(system_resource) "Elasticity (system resource)") (a process that allows a client to use more computing in times of high application usage, and then scale down to reduce costs when there is less traffic). These cloud computing [web services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_service "Web service") provide various services related to networking, compute, storage, [middleware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleware "Middleware"), [IoT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_of_things "Internet of things") and other processing capacity, as well as [software tools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_tools "Software tools") via AWS [server farms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Server_farm "Server farm"). This frees clients from managing, scaling, and patching hardware and operating systems.

One of the foundational services is [Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Elastic_Compute_Cloud "Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud") (EC2), which allows users to have at their disposal a [virtual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtualization "Virtualization") [cluster of computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_cluster "Computer cluster"), with extremely high availability, which can be interacted with over the Internet via [REST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/REST "REST") APIs, a [CLI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Command-line_interface "Command-line interface") or the AWS console. AWS's virtual computers emulate most of the attributes of a real computer, including hardware [central processing units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") (CPUs) and [graphics processing units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphics_processing_unit "Graphics processing unit") (GPUs) for processing; local/[RAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random-access_memory "Random-access memory") memory; [hard-disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_disk_drive "Hard disk drive") (HDD)/[SSD storage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid-state_drive "Solid-state drive"); a choice of [operating systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system"); networking; and pre-loaded application software such as [web servers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_server "Web server"), [databases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Database "Database"), and [customer relationship management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Customer_relationship_management "Customer relationship management") (CRM).

AWS services are delivered to customers via a network of AWS server farms located throughout the world. Fees are based on a combination of usage (known as a "Pay-as-you-go" model), hardware, operating system, software, and networking features chosen by the subscriber requiring various degrees of [availability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Availability_(system) "Availability (system)"), [redundancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redundancy_(engineering) "Redundancy (engineering)"), [security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_security "Computer security"), and service options. Subscribers can pay for a single virtual AWS computer, a dedicated physical computer, or clusters of either.[[7]](#cite_note-AWSagreement-9) Amazon provides select portions of security for subscribers (e.g. physical security of the data centers) while other aspects of security are the responsibility of the subscriber (e.g. account management, vulnerability scanning, patching). AWS operates from many global geographical regions, including nine in North America.[[8]](#cite_note-GlobalInfrastructure-10)

Amazon markets AWS to subscribers as a way of obtaining large-scale computing capacity more quickly and cheaply than building an actual physical server farm.[[9]](#cite_note-11) All services are billed based on usage, but each service measures usage in varying ways. As of 2023 Q1, AWS has 31% market share for cloud infrastructure while the next two competitors [Microsoft Azure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Azure "Microsoft Azure") and [Google Cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Cloud_Platform "Google Cloud Platform") have 25%, and 11% respectively, according to Synergy Research Group.[[10]](#cite_note-12)[[11]](#cite_note-13) AWS was the first cloud provider to build infrastructure specifically for U.S. government with respect to security and compliance requirements (2011; launched AWS GovCloud), accredited to support classified workloads (2014; launched AWS Top Secret), and achieve accreditation across all U.S. government data classifications (2017; launched AWS Secret).[[12]](#cite_note-auto3-14)[[13]](#cite_note-15)

## Services

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Services")]

Main articles: [Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Elastic_Compute_Cloud "Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud") and [Amazon S3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_S3 "Amazon S3")

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit) AWS comprises over 200[[14]](#cite_note-techradar-16) products and services including [computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computation "Computation"), [storage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Elastic_File_System "Amazon Elastic File System"), [networking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_network "Computer network"), [database](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Database "Database"), [analytics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytics "Analytics"), [application services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Application_service_provider "Application service provider"), [deployment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_deployment "Software deployment"), [management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_management "Systems management"), [machine learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning"),[[15]](#cite_note-17) [mobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_application_development "Mobile application development"), [developer tools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_tool "Programming tool"), RobOps and tools for the [Internet of Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_of_Things "Internet of Things"). The most popular include [Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Elastic_Compute_Cloud "Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud") (EC2), [Amazon Simple Storage Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Simple_Storage_Service "Amazon Simple Storage Service") (Amazon S3), Amazon Connect, and [AWS Lambda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AWS_Lambda "AWS Lambda") (a [serverless function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serverless_computing "Serverless computing") that can perform arbitrary code written in any [language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_language "Programming language") that can be configured to be triggered by hundreds of [events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Event_(computing) "Event (computing)"), including [HTTP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP "HTTP") calls).[[16]](#cite_note-mostpopularservices-18)

Services expose functionality through APIs for clients to use in their applications. These APIs are accessed over HTTP, using the [REST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/REST "REST") architectural style and [SOAP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SOAP "SOAP") protocol for older APIs and exclusively [JSON](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JSON "JSON") for newer ones. Clients can interact with these APIs in various ways, including from the AWS console (a website), by using [SDKs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_development_kit "Software development kit") written in various languages (such as [Python](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python_(programming_language) "Python (programming language)"), [Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_(programming_language) "Java (programming language)"), and [JavaScript](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JavaScript "JavaScript")), or by making direct REST calls.

### Founding (2000–2005)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Founding (2000–2005)")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/5/5d/Amazon.com_web_services_2002.jpg/250px-Amazon.com_web_services_2002.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Amazon.com_web_services_2002.jpg)

Early AWS "building blocks" logo

The genesis of AWS came in the early 2000s. After building *Merchant.com*, Amazon's e-commerce-as-a-service platform that offers third-party retailers a way to build their own web-stores, Amazon pursued [service-oriented architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Service-oriented_architecture "Service-oriented architecture") as a means to scale its engineering operations,[[17]](#cite_note-horsemouth-19)[[18]](#cite_note-foraws-20)[[19]](#cite_note-tcaws-21)[[20]](#cite_note-crnaws-22)[[21]](#cite_note-hilabs-23)[[22]](#cite_note-vdynamo-24)[[23]](#cite_note-vogels-25) led by then [CTO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_technology_officer "Chief technology officer") Allan Vermeulen.[[24]](#cite_note-brad-26)

Around the same time frame, Amazon was frustrated with the speed of its software engineering, and sought to implement various recommendations put forth by Matt Round, an engineering leader at the time, including maximization of autonomy for engineering teams, adoption of [REST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representational_state_transfer "Representational state transfer"), standardization of infrastructure, removal of gate-keeping decision-makers (bureaucracy), and [continuous deployment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_deployment "Continuous deployment"). He also called for increasing the percentage of the time engineers spent building the software rather than doing other tasks.[[25]](#cite_note-velocity-27) Amazon created "a shared [IT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_Technology "Information Technology") platform" so its engineering organizations, which were spending 70% of their time on "undifferentiated heavy-lifting" such as IT and infrastructure problems, could focus on customer-facing innovation instead.[[26]](#cite_note-28)[[27]](#cite_note-aselip-29) Besides, in dealing with unusual peak traffic patterns, especially during [the holiday season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics_of_Christmas "Economics of Christmas"), by migrating services to commodity Linux hardware and relying on [open source software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_source_software "Open source software"), Amazon's Infrastructure team, led by Tom Killalea,[[28]](#cite_note-tompeak-30) Amazon's first [CISO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CISO "CISO"),[[29]](#cite_note-31) had already run its data centers and associated services in a "fast, reliable, cheap" way.[[28]](#cite_note-tompeak-30)

In July 2002 Amazon.com Web Services, managed by Colin Bryar,[[30]](#cite_note-32) launched its first [web services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_service "Web service"), opening up the Amazon.com platform to all developers.[[31]](#cite_note-33) Over one hundred applications were built on top of it by 2004.[[32]](#cite_note-tomlinux-34) This unexpected developer interest took Amazon by surprise and convinced them that developers were "hungry for more".[[27]](#cite_note-aselip-29)

By the summer of 2003, [Andy Jassy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Jassy "Andy Jassy") had taken over Bryar's portfolio[[33]](#cite_note-working-35) at [Rick Dalzell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Dalzell "Rick Dalzell")'s behest, after Vermeulen, who was Bezos' first pick, declined the offer.[[24]](#cite_note-brad-26) Jassy subsequently mapped out the vision for an "Internet [OS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating_System "Operating System")"[[17]](#cite_note-horsemouth-19)[[19]](#cite_note-tcaws-21)[[21]](#cite_note-hilabs-23)[[34]](#cite_note-telaws-36) made up of foundational infrastructure primitives that alleviated key impediments to shipping software applications faster.[[17]](#cite_note-horsemouth-19)[[18]](#cite_note-foraws-20)[[19]](#cite_note-tcaws-21)[[21]](#cite_note-hilabs-23)[[23]](#cite_note-vogels-25) By fall 2003,[[17]](#cite_note-horsemouth-19)[[19]](#cite_note-tcaws-21) [databases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Databases "Databases"), [storage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_storage "Cloud storage"), and [compute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compute "Compute") were identified as the first set of infrastructure pieces that Amazon should launch.[[17]](#cite_note-horsemouth-19)[[19]](#cite_note-tcaws-21)[[27]](#cite_note-aselip-29)

Jeff Barr, an early AWS employee, credits himself, Vermeulen, Jassy, Bezos, and a few others for coming up with the idea that would evolve into [EC2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_EC2 "Amazon EC2"), [S3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_S3 "Amazon S3"), and [RDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_RDS "Amazon RDS");[[35]](#cite_note-37) Jassy recalls the idea was the result of brainstorming for about a week with "ten of the best [technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_engineering "Software engineering") minds and ten of the best [product management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_management "Product management") minds" on about ten different Internet applications and the most primitive building blocks required to build them.[[21]](#cite_note-hilabs-23) [Werner Vogels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werner_Vogels "Werner Vogels") cites Amazon's desire to make the process of "invent, launch, reinvent, relaunch, start over, rinse, repeat" as fast as it could was leading them to break down [organizational structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_company "Big company") with "two-pizza teams"[[c]](#cite_note-39) and [application structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_architecture "Software architecture") with [distributed systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_computing "Distributed computing");[[d]](#cite_note-40) and that these changes ultimately paved way for the formation of AWS[[23]](#cite_note-vogels-25) and its mission "to expose all of the atomic-level pieces of the Amazon.com platform".[[37]](#cite_note-41) According to [Brewster Kahle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brewster_Kahle "Brewster Kahle"), co-founder of [Alexa Internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexa_Internet "Alexa Internet"), which was acquired by Amazon in 1999, his start-up's compute infrastructure helped Amazon solve its [big data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_data "Big data") problems and later informed the innovations that underpinned AWS.[[38]](#cite_note-42)

Jassy assembled a founding team of 57 employees from a mix of engineering and business backgrounds to kick-start these initiatives,[[21]](#cite_note-hilabs-23)[[20]](#cite_note-crnaws-22) with a majority of the hires coming from outside the company.[[21]](#cite_note-hilabs-23) They included Jeff Lawson, the [Twilio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilio "Twilio") CEO;[[39]](#cite_note-43) Adam Selipsky, the [Tableau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tableau_Inc "Tableau Inc") CEO;[[40]](#cite_note-44)[[41]](#cite_note-45) and Mikhail Seregine,[[42]](#cite_note-46) a co-founder at [Outschool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outschool "Outschool").

In late 2003, the concept for compute,[[e]](#cite_note-48) which would later launch as [EC2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_EC2 "Amazon EC2"), was reformulated when Chris Pinkham and Benjamin Black presented a paper internally describing a vision for Amazon's retail computing infrastructure that was completely standardized, completely automated, and would rely extensively on web services for services such as storage and would draw on internal work already underway. Near the end of their paper, they mentioned the possibility of selling access to virtual servers as a service, proposing the company could generate revenue from the new infrastructure investment.[[44]](#cite_note-PinkhamBlack2003Paper-49)[*[unreliable source?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources")*] Thereafter Pinkham, [Willem van Biljon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willem_van_Biljon "Willem van Biljon"), and lead developer Christopher Brown developed the Amazon EC2 service, with a team in [Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town "Cape Town"), South Africa.[[45]](#cite_note-50)

In October 2004, Amazon released Alexa Web Information Service (AWIS) as beta.[[46]](#cite_note-51) In November 2004, AWS launched its first [infrastructure service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IaaS "IaaS"), as beta: [Simple Queue Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Simple_Queue_Service "Amazon Simple Queue Service") (SQS).[[47]](#cite_note-52)[[48]](#cite_note-53)[[49]](#cite_note-54), and officially launched in July 2006.[[50]](#cite_note-55)[[51]](#cite_note-auto2-56)

Amazon Elastic Block Store

On March 14, 2006, AWS launched [Amazon S3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_S3 "Amazon S3") [cloud storage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_storage "Cloud storage")[[52]](#cite_note-pieday-57), and that was the first AWS' IaaS that was generally available,[[51]](#cite_note-auto2-56) followed by EC2 in August 2006.[[53]](#cite_note-58)[[54]](#cite_note-ec2l-59) Pi Corporation, a startup [Paul Maritz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Maritz "Paul Maritz") co-founded, was the first beta-user of [EC2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Elastic_Compute_Cloud "Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud") outside of Amazon,[[21]](#cite_note-hilabs-23) while [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft") was among EC2's first enterprise customers.[[55]](#cite_note-60) Later that year [SmugMug](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SmugMug "SmugMug"), one of the early AWS adopters, attributed savings of around [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USD "USD")400,000 in storage costs to S3.[[56]](#cite_note-61) According to Vogels, S3 was built with 8 [microservices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microservices "Microservices") when it launched in 2006 and had over 300 microservices by 2022.[[57]](#cite_note-62)

In September 2007, AWS announced its annual *Start-up Challenge*, a contest with prizes worth [$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USD "USD")100,000 for entrepreneurs and software developers in the US using AWS services such as S3 and EC2 to build their businesses.[[58]](#cite_note-63) The first edition saw participation from [Justin.tv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justin.tv "Justin.tv"),[[59]](#cite_note-schall1-64) which Amazon later acquired in 2014.[[60]](#cite_note-acqtwi-65) [Ooyala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ooyala "Ooyala"), an online media company,[[61]](#cite_note-66) was the eventual winner.[[59]](#cite_note-schall1-64)

AWS offers, as of June 16, 2022[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit), two block-storage options: the EC2 Instance Store and the Elastic Block Store (EBS).[[62]](#cite_note-67) Some Amazon EBS features that help with data management, backups, and performance tuning include:

* EBS volume tagging to allow the user to find and filter EBS resources on the Amazon Console and CLI.[[63]](#cite_note-68)
* Software-level RAID arrays to enable creation of groups of EBS volumes with high performance network throughput between them, using the standard [RAID](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAID "RAID") protocol.[[64]](#cite_note-69)

Additional AWS services from this period include [SimpleDB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_SimpleDB "Amazon SimpleDB"), [Mechanical Turk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Mechanical_Turk "Amazon Mechanical Turk"), [Elastic Beanstalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AWS_Elastic_Beanstalk "AWS Elastic Beanstalk"), [Relational Database Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Relational_Database_Service "Amazon Relational Database Service"), [DynamoDB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_DynamoDB "Amazon DynamoDB"), [CloudWatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Elastic_Compute_Cloud#Amazon_CloudWatch "Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud"), Simple Workflow, [CloudFront](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_CloudFront "Amazon CloudFront"), and Availability Zones.

### Growth (2010–2015)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Growth (2010–2015)")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/AWSSummit2013NYC2.JPG/250px-AWSSummit2013NYC2.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:AWSSummit2013NYC2.JPG)

AWS Summit 2013 event in NYC

In November 2010, it was reported that all of Amazon.com's retail sites had migrated to AWS.[[65]](#cite_note-70) Prior to 2012, AWS was considered a part of Amazon.com and so its revenue was not delineated in Amazon financial statements. In that year industry watchers for the first time estimated AWS revenue to be over $1.5 billion.[[66]](#cite_note-71)

On November 27, 2012, AWS hosted its first major annual conference, *re:Invent* with a focus on AWS's partners and ecosystem,[[67]](#cite_note-72) with over 150 sessions.[[68]](#cite_note-freinventblog-73) The three-day event was held in Las Vegas because of its relatively cheaper connectivity with locations across the United States and the rest of the world.[[69]](#cite_note-74) Andy Jassy and Werner Vogels presented keynotes, with [Jeff Bezos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Bezos "Jeff Bezos") joining Vogels for a fireside chat.[[70]](#cite_note-net1-75) AWS opened early registrations at [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USD "USD")1,099 per head for their customers[[68]](#cite_note-freinventblog-73) from over 190 countries.[[71]](#cite_note-76) On stage with Andy Jassy at the event which saw around 6000 attendees, [Reed Hastings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reed_Hastings "Reed Hastings"), CEO at [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix"), announced plans to migrate 100% of Netflix's infrastructure to AWS.[[70]](#cite_note-net1-75)

To support industry-wide training and skills standardization, AWS began offering a certification program for computer engineers, on April 30, 2013, to highlight expertise in cloud computing.[[72]](#cite_note-77) Later that year, in October, AWS launched *Activate*, a program for start-ups worldwide to leverage AWS credits, third-party integrations, and free access to AWS experts to help build their business.[[73]](#cite_note-78)

In 2014, AWS launched its partner network, AWS Partner Network (APN), which is focused on helping AWS-based companies grow and scale the success of their business with close collaboration and best practices.[[74]](#cite_note-79)[[75]](#cite_note-80)

In October 2014, [Amazon Aurora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Aurora "Amazon Aurora") was launched.[[76]](#cite_note-81)

In January 2015, Amazon Web Services acquired [Annapurna Labs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annapurna_Labs "Annapurna Labs"), an Israel-based microelectronics company for a reported US$350–370M.[[77]](#cite_note-reut_Amaz-82)[[78]](#cite_note-extr_Amaz-83)

In April 2015, Amazon.com reported AWS was profitable, with sales of $1.57 billion in the first quarter of the year and $265 million of operating income. Founder [Jeff Bezos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Bezos "Jeff Bezos") described it as a fast-growing $5 billion business; analysts described it as "surprisingly more profitable than forecast".[[79]](#cite_note-84) In October, Amazon.com said in its Q3 earnings report that AWS's operating income was $521 million, with operating margins at 25 percent. AWS's 2015 Q3 revenue was $2.1 billion, a 78% increase from 2014's Q3 revenue of $1.17 billion.[[80]](#cite_note-85) 2015 Q4 revenue for the AWS segment increased 69.5% y/y to $2.4 billion with a 28.5% operating margin, giving AWS a $9.6 billion run rate. In 2015, [Gartner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gartner "Gartner") estimated that AWS customers are deploying 10x more infrastructure on AWS than the combined adoption of the next 14 providers.[[81]](#cite_note-86)

### Since 2016

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Since 2016")]

In 2016 Q1, revenue was $2.57 billion with net income of $604 million, a 64% increase over 2015 Q1 that resulted in AWS being more profitable than Amazon's North American retail business for the first time.[[82]](#cite_note-87) Jassy was thereafter promoted to CEO of the division.[[83]](#cite_note-CEO_Andy_Jassy-88) Around the same time, Amazon experienced a 42% rise in stock value as a result of increased earnings, of which AWS contributed 56% to corporate profits.[[84]](#cite_note-89)

AWS had $17.46 billion in annual revenue in 2017.[[85]](#cite_note-auto1-90) By the end of 2020, the number had grown to [$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USD "USD")46 billion.[[86]](#cite_note-2020sales-91) Reflecting the success of AWS, Jassy's annual compensation in 2017 hit nearly $36 million.[[87]](#cite_note-auto-92)

In January 2018, Amazon launched a unified [autoscaling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoscaling "Autoscaling") service on AWS.[[88]](#cite_note-93)[[89]](#cite_note-94) This new service unifies and builds on AWS existing, service-specific, scaling features like EC2 Auto Scaling groups, that was launched in August 2006.[[90]](#cite_note-95)

In November 2018, AWS announced customized ARM cores for use in its servers.[[91]](#cite_note-96) Also in November 2018, AWS created ground stations to communicate with customers' satellites.[[92]](#cite_note-97)

In 2019, AWS reported 37% yearly growth and accounted for 12% of Amazon's revenue (up from 11% in 2018).[[93]](#cite_note-98)

In April 2021, AWS reported 32% yearly growth and accounted for 32% of $41.8 billion cloud market in Q1 2021.[[94]](#cite_note-99)

In January 2022, AWS joined the MACH Alliance, a non-profit enterprise technology advocacy group.[[95]](#cite_note-100)

In June 2022, it was reported that in 2019 Capital One had not secured their AWS resources properly, and was subject to a data breach by a former AWS employee. The employee was convicted of hacking into the company's cloud servers to steal customer data and use computer power to mine cryptocurrency. The ex-employee was able to download the personal information of more than 100 million Capital One customers.[[96]](#cite_note-101)

In June 2022, AWS announced they had launched the AWS Snowcone, a small computing device, to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") on the [Axiom Mission 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axiom_Mission_1 "Axiom Mission 1").[[97]](#cite_note-102)

In September 2023, AWS announced it would become AI startup [Anthropic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropic "Anthropic")'s primary cloud provider. Amazon has committed to investing up to $4 billion in Anthropic and will have a minority ownership position in the company.[[98]](#cite_note-103) AWS also announced the GA of [Amazon Bedrock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Bedrock "Amazon Bedrock"), a fully managed service that makes foundation models (FMs) from leading AI companies available through a single application programming interface (API)[[99]](#cite_note-104)

In April 2024, AWS announced a new service called Deadline Cloud, which lets customers set up, deploy and scale up graphics and visual effects rendering pipelines on AWS cloud infrastructure.[[100]](#cite_note-105)

In July 2024, AWS won a $1.3 billion (A$2 billion) contract with Australia's government to build a top-secret cloud service. The service included a partnership with the [Australian Signals Directorate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Signals_Directorate "Australian Signals Directorate") (ASD). The ASD director general Rachel Noble said the service would "provide a state-of-the-art collaborative space for our intelligence and defense community to store and access top-secret data”.[[101]](#cite_note-106)

In December 2024, AWS announced Amazon Nova, its own family of [foundation models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foundation_model "Foundation model"). These models, offered through Amazon Bedrock, are designed for various tasks including content generation, video understanding, and building agentic applications. They are available in six different sizes.[[102]](#cite_note-107) At the end of 2024, AWS announced Project Rainier, a massive one-of-a-kind machine "designed to usher in the next generation of AI."[[103]](#cite_note-108)

In February 2026, India's [National Informatics Centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Informatics_Centre "National Informatics Centre") (NIC), a department under the [Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_Electronics_and_Information_Technology "Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology"), announced deployment of [AWS Outposts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AWS_Outposts?action=edit&redlink=1 "AWS Outposts (page does not exist)") within its data centers as part of the government's Meghraj 2.0 hybrid cloud initiative, working with Indian data center provider Yotta Data Services. The deployment enables sensitive government workloads to remain within NIC's physical infrastructure while accessing AWS cloud services including Amazon EKS, Amazon RDS, and Amazon S3.[[104]](#cite_note-109)

In March and April of 2026, during the [2026 Iran War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Iran_War "2026 Iran War"), Iranian drone and missile strikes damaged AWS data centers in the United Arab Emirates (me-central-1) and Bahrain (me-south-1) regions, in the first deliberate military targeting of a commercial data center. Iran claimed the data centers hosted US military workloads. AWS advised customers to migrate to other regions.[[105]](#cite_note-110)[[106]](#cite_note-:3-111)

On 30 June 2026, AWS Secret Cloud for Industry (ASCI) was made generally available. It holds a Provisional Authorization at Impact Level 6 from the Defense Information Systems Agency and uses the same Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) compliance framework that cleared defense contractors already use for on-premises classified systems. Northrop Grumman was the first defense contractor to deploy classified workloads on ASCI. To speed up the migration and to attract customers AWS launched ASCI Accelerator Initiative.[[12]](#cite_note-auto3-14) The U.S. Intelligence Community (IC) launched IC Accelerated Modernization Framework (ICAMF) which subsidizes transfer to AWS from on-site systems. ASCI provides physically and logically isolated environment purpose-built to meet the most demanding security and compliance requirements.[[107]](#cite_note-112) They also created AWS [Forward Deployed Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward_deployed_engineer "Forward deployed engineer") (FDE) organization. It embeds *AWS frontier teams*[[108]](#cite_note-113)—working with purpose-built agents—directly inside customer teams (business, engineering, and security teams) to build and deploy production AI systems with their data, governance, and processes.[[109]](#cite_note-114)

Main article: [Timeline of Amazon Web Services § Outages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Amazon_Web_Services#Outages "Timeline of Amazon Web Services")

* On April 20, 2011, AWS suffered a major outage. Parts of the Elastic Block Store service became "stuck" and could not fulfill read/write requests. It took at least two days for the service to be fully restored.[[123]](#cite_note-128)
* On June 29, 2012, several websites that rely on Amazon Web Services were taken offline due to [a severe storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/June_2012_North_American_derecho "June 2012 North American derecho") in [Northern Virginia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Virginia "Northern Virginia"), where AWS's largest data center cluster is located.[[124]](#cite_note-129)
* On October 22, 2012, a major outage occurred, affecting many sites including [Reddit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reddit "Reddit"), [Foursquare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foursquare_City_Guide "Foursquare City Guide"), and [Pinterest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pinterest "Pinterest"). The cause was a [memory leak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_leak "Memory leak") bug in an operational data collection agent.[[125]](#cite_note-130)
* On December 24, 2012, AWS suffered another outage causing websites such as [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix") to be unavailable for customers in the Northeastern United States.[[126]](#cite_note-131) AWS cited their [Elastic Load Balancing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elastic_Load_Balancing "Elastic Load Balancing") service as the cause.[[127]](#cite_note-132)
* On February 28, 2017, AWS experienced a massive outage of S3 services in its Northern Virginia region. A majority of websites that relied on AWS S3 either hung or stalled, and Amazon reported within five hours that AWS was fully online again.[[128]](#cite_note-133) No data has been reported to have been lost due to the outage. The outage was caused by a [human error](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_error "Human error") made while [debugging](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debugging "Debugging"), that resulted in removing more server capacity than intended, which caused a domino effect of outages.[[129]](#cite_note-134)
* On November 25, 2020, AWS experienced several hours of outage on the [Kinesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Kinesis "Amazon Kinesis") service in North Virginia (US-East-1) region. Other services relying on Kinesis were also affected.[[130]](#cite_note-135)[[131]](#cite_note-136)
* On December 7, 2021, an outage mainly affected the Eastern United States, disrupting delivery service and streaming.[[132]](#cite_note-137)
* On October 20, 2025, AWS suffered a major outage, resulting in platforms including [Duolingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duolingo "Duolingo"), [Snapchat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snapchat "Snapchat"), [Canva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canva "Canva"),[[133]](#cite_note-138) [Reddit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reddit "Reddit"), [Canvas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instructure "Instructure"),[[134]](#cite_note-139) [Coinbase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coinbase "Coinbase"), [Roblox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roblox "Roblox"), [Fortnite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortnite "Fortnite"), and [Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_(company) "Amazon (company)") being down.[[135]](#cite_note-140)[[136]](#cite_note-141)[[137]](#cite_note-142)

## Availability and topology

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Availability and topology")]

As of October 2025,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit) AWS has distinct operations in 38 geographical "regions":[[8]](#cite_note-GlobalInfrastructure-10) nine in [North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_America "North America"), two in [South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America "South America"), nine in [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe"), four in the [Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_East "Middle East"), one in Africa, thirteen in the [Asia–Pacific](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia–Pacific "Asia–Pacific"), and three in Australia and New Zealand.

Most AWS regions are enabled by default for AWS accounts. Regions introduced after 20 March 2019 are considered to be *opt-in* regions, requiring a user to explicitly enable them in order for the region to be usable in the account. For opt-in regions, Identity and Access Management (IAM) resources such as users and roles are only propagated to the regions that are enabled.[[138]](#cite_note-143)

Each region is wholly contained within a single country and all of its data and services stay within the designated region.[[7]](#cite_note-AWSagreement-9) Each region has multiple "Availability Zones",[[8]](#cite_note-GlobalInfrastructure-10) which consist of one or more discrete [data centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_center "Data center"), each with [redundant power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emergency_power_system "Emergency power system"), networking, and connectivity, housed in separate facilities. Availability Zones do not automatically provide additional scalability or redundancy within a region, since they are intentionally isolated from each other to prevent [outages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_outage "Network outage") from spreading between zones. Several services can operate across Availability Zones (e.g., S3, [DynamoDB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_DynamoDB "Amazon DynamoDB")) while others can be configured to replicate across zones to spread demand and avoid [downtime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Downtime "Downtime") from failures.

As of December 2014,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit) Amazon Web Services operated an estimated 1.4 million servers across 11 regions and 28 availability zones.[[139]](#cite_note-144) The global network of AWS Edge locations consists of over 700 points of presence worldwide, including locations in North America, Europe, Asia, Australia and New Zealand, Africa, and South America.The AWS Cloud spans 120 Availability Zones within 38 Geographic Regions, with announced plans for 10 more Availability Zones and 3 more AWS Regions in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, Chile, and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.[[8]](#cite_note-GlobalInfrastructure-10)

As of March 2024,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit) AWS had announced the planned launch of six additional regions in Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Thailand, Saudi Arabia, and the European Union.[[8]](#cite_note-GlobalInfrastructure-10) In mid March 2023, Amazon Web Services signed a cooperation agreement with the New Zealand Government to build large data centers in New Zealand.[[140]](#cite_note-145)

### Environmental footprint

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Environmental footprint")]

In 2014, AWS claimed its aim was to achieve [100% renewable energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/100%25_renewable_energy "100% renewable energy") usage in the future.[[153]](#cite_note-158) In the United States, AWS's partnerships with renewable energy providers include Community Energy of Virginia, to support the US East region;[[154]](#cite_note-burt2015-159) Pattern Development, in January 2015, to construct and operate Amazon [Wind Farm Fowler Ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fowler_Ridge_Wind_Farm "Fowler Ridge Wind Farm");[[155]](#cite_note-160) [Iberdrola Renewables](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avangrid "Avangrid"), LLC, in July 2015, to construct and operate Amazon Wind Farm US East; [EDP Renewables North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EDP_Renewables_North_America "EDP Renewables North America"), in November 2015, to construct and operate Amazon Wind Farm US Central;[[156]](#cite_note-161) and [Tesla Motors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tesla_Motors "Tesla Motors"), to apply battery storage technology to address power needs in the US West (Northern California) region.[[154]](#cite_note-burt2015-159)

In 2016, [Greenpeace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenpeace "Greenpeace") assessed major tech companies—including cloud services providers like AWS, [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft"), [Oracle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oracle_Corporation "Oracle Corporation"), [Google](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google "Google"), [IBM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM "IBM"), [Salesforce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salesforce "Salesforce") and [Rackspace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rackspace "Rackspace")—based on their level of "clean energy" usage. Greenpeace evaluated companies on their mix of renewable-energy sources; transparency; renewable-energy commitment and policies; energy efficiency and greenhouse-gas mitigation; renewable-energy procurement; and advocacy. The group gave AWS an overall "C" grade. Greenpeace credited AWS for its advances toward greener computing in recent years and its plans to launch multiple wind and solar farms across the United States. The organization stated that Amazon is opaque about its [carbon footprint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_footprint "Carbon footprint").[[157]](#cite_note-162)

In January 2021, AWS joined an industry pledge to achieve [climate neutrality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_neutrality "Carbon neutrality") of data centers by 2030, the [Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_Neutral_Data_Centre_Pact "Climate Neutral Data Centre Pact").[[158]](#cite_note-163) As of 2023, Amazon as a whole is the largest corporate purchaser of renewable energy in the world, a position it has held since 2020, and has a global portfolio of over 20 GW of renewable energy capacity.[[159]](#cite_note-164) In 2022, 90% of all Amazon operations, including data centers, were powered by renewables.[[160]](#cite_note-165) In 2024, AWS paid $650 million for a data center[[161]](#cite_note-166) at the 2.5 GW [Susquehanna nuclear power plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susquehanna_Steam_Electric_Station "Susquehanna Steam Electric Station"), connected at 300 MW. In 2025, AWS signed an $18 billion [power purchase agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_purchase_agreement "Power purchase agreement") with the station for 840—1,200 MW in 2029 and 1,680—1,920 MW in 2032, continuing to 2042. The power increase depends on Amazon's expansion of the data center.[[162]](#cite_note-pat-167)

### Denaturalization protest

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Denaturalization protest")]

US [Department of Homeland Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Homeland_Security "Department of Homeland Security") has employed the software ATLAS, which runs on Amazon Cloud. It scanned more than 16.5 million records of naturalized Americans and flagged approximately 124,000 of them for manual analysis and review by [USCIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USCIS "USCIS") officers regarding [denaturalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denaturalization "Denaturalization").[[163]](#cite_note-168)[[164]](#cite_note-169) Some of the scanned data came from the [Terrorist Screening Database](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrorist_Screening_Database "Terrorist Screening Database") and the [National Crime Information Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Crime_Information_Center "National Crime Information Center"). The algorithm and the criteria for the algorithm were secret. Amazon faced protests from its own employees and activists for the anti-migrant collaboration with authorities.[[165]](#cite_note-170)

## Security incidents

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Security incidents")]

### Amazon Q Developer Extension supply-chain vulnerability (2025)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Amazon Q Developer Extension supply-chain vulnerability (2025)")]

In July 2025, a security researcher disclosed a supply-chain vulnerability in the Amazon Q Developer Extension (version 1.84) for Visual Studio Code.[[173]](#cite_note-:1-178) The issue involved a malicious pull request to the project's GitHub repository, which introduced a prompt instructing the AI assistant to delete local files and AWS resources.[[174]](#cite_note-:2-179)[[173]](#cite_note-:1-178) AWS acknowledged the issue in Security Bulletin AWS‑2025‑015 and released version 1.85 to remove the injected prompt. The company stated that no customer systems or data were affected.[[175]](#cite_note-180) However, critics including Corey Quinn, writing in Last Week in AWS, questioned the transparency of the response, noting the absence of a changelog entry, a CVE assignment, or a public statement beyond the bulletin.[[174]](#cite_note-:2-179)

### Log4Shell Hot Patch vulnerability

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Log4Shell Hot Patch vulnerability")]

In response to the [Log4Shell vulnerability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log4Shell "Log4Shell"), AWS released hot patch solutions to mitigate risks in Java applications across various environments, including standalone servers, Kubernetes clusters, and Elastic Container Service (ECS). These patches were designed for both AWS and non-AWS environments. However, researchers from Unit 42 at [Palo Alto Networks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palo_Alto_Networks "Palo Alto Networks") identified critical security flaws in these patches that could be exploited for container escape and privilege escalation, potentially granting attackers unauthorized root-level access to the host system. AWS addressed these vulnerabilities by releasing updated patches on April 19, 2022. Users who deployed the initial patches were advised to upgrade to the latest versions to mitigate security risks.[[176]](#cite_note-181)

### Application Load Balancer security issue

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Application Load Balancer security issue")]

In April 2024, security researchers from Miggo security identified a configuration vulnerability in AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB) that could allow attackers to bypass access controls and compromise web applications. The issue stemmed from how some users configured ALB's authentication handoff to third-party services, potentially enabling unauthorized access to application data. On July 11, 2024, AWS confirmed the issue affecting its customers, and on July 19, 2024, AWS updated its documentation accordingly to recommend more secure implementation practices.[[177]](#cite_note-182)[[178]](#cite_note-183)

In 2026, Amazon Web Services (AWS) data center infrastructure in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain experienced service disruptions following reported drone strikes in the region. According to Datacenter Dynamics and Reuters, some facilities were affected, resulting in partial damage to physical infrastructure and temporary reductions in service availability for enterprise customers. reports indicated that full recovery of services in the affected regions could take several months, with some services being moved to other cloud regions.[[179]](#cite_note-184)[[180]](#cite_note-185)[[181]](#cite_note-186)

## Pricing

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Pricing")]

### Data transfer charges

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Data transfer charges")]

AWS applies charges for data transferred both between Availability Zones within the same region (inter-AZ) and across different geographic regions (inter-region). The pricing structure is influenced by several factors, including the source and destination of the data, the specific AWS services in use, and the underlying networking architecture.[[185]](#cite_note-190)[[186]](#cite_note-:0-191) Various services implement different data transfer models, and the choice of communication method—such as VPC Peering,[[187]](#cite_note-192) Transit Gateway,[[188]](#cite_note-193) or AWS PrivateLink[[189]](#cite_note-194)—can also affect the overall cost.[[186]](#cite_note-:0-191)

The company has business operations across the world. AWS is headquartered in Seattle, Washington, the US.

The company operates in the IT services and IT consulting industry and offers cloud infrastructure services to customers worldwide.

**Amazon Web Services, Inc.** (**AWS**) is a subsidiary of [Amazon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_(company) "Amazon (company)") that provides [on-demand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_as_a_service "Software as a service") [cloud computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_computing "Cloud computing") [platforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computing_platform "Computing platform") and [APIs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/API "API") to individuals, companies, and governments, on a metered, pay-as-you-go basis.

Clients often use this in combination with [autoscaling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elasticity_(system_resource) "Elasticity (system resource)") (a process that allows a client to use more computing in times of high application usage, and then scale down to reduce costs when there is less traffic). These cloud computing [web services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_service "Web service") provide various services related to networking, compute, storage, [middleware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleware "Middleware"), [IoT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_of_things "Internet of things") and other processing capacity, as well as [software tools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_tools "Software tools") via AWS [server farms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Server_farm "Server farm"). This frees clients from managing, scaling, and patching hardware and operating systems.

One of the foundational services is [Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Elastic_Compute_Cloud "Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud") (EC2), which allows users to have at their disposal a [virtual](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Virtualization "Virtualization") [cluster of computers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_cluster "Computer cluster"), with extremely high availability, which can be interacted with over the Internet via [REST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/REST "REST") APIs, a [CLI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Command-line_interface "Command-line interface") or the AWS console. AWS's virtual computers emulate most of the attributes of a real computer, including hardware [central processing units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") (CPUs) and [graphics processing units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphics_processing_unit "Graphics processing unit") (GPUs) for processing; local/[RAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random-access_memory "Random-access memory") memory; [hard-disk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_disk_drive "Hard disk drive") (HDD)/[SSD storage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid-state_drive "Solid-state drive"); a choice of [operating systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating_system "Operating system"); networking; and pre-loaded application software such as [web servers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_server "Web server"), [databases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Database "Database"), and [customer relationship management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Customer_relationship_management "Customer relationship management") (CRM).

AWS services are delivered to customers via a network of AWS server farms located throughout the world. Fees are based on a combination of usage (known as a "Pay-as-you-go" model), hardware, operating system, software, and networking features chosen by the subscriber requiring various degrees of [availability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Availability_(system) "Availability (system)"), [redundancy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redundancy_(engineering) "Redundancy (engineering)"), [security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_security "Computer security"), and service options. Subscribers can pay for a single virtual AWS computer, a dedicated physical computer, or clusters of either.[[7]](#cite_note-AWSagreement-9) Amazon provides select portions of security for subscribers (e.g. physical security of the data centers) while other aspects of security are the responsibility of the subscriber (e.g. account management, vulnerability scanning, patching). AWS operates from many global geographical regions, including nine in North America.[[8]](#cite_note-GlobalInfrastructure-10)

Amazon markets AWS to subscribers as a way of obtaining large-scale computing capacity more quickly and cheaply than building an actual physical server farm.[[9]](#cite_note-11) All services are billed based on usage, but each service measures usage in varying ways. As of 2023 Q1, AWS has 31% market share for cloud infrastructure while the next two competitors [Microsoft Azure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft_Azure "Microsoft Azure") and [Google Cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google_Cloud_Platform "Google Cloud Platform") have 25%, and 11% respectively, according to Synergy Research Group.[[10]](#cite_note-12)[[11]](#cite_note-13) AWS was the first cloud provider to build infrastructure specifically for U.S. government with respect to security and compliance requirements (2011; launched AWS GovCloud), accredited to support classified workloads (2014; launched AWS Top Secret), and achieve accreditation across all U.S. government data classifications (2017; launched AWS Secret).[[12]](#cite_note-auto3-14)[[13]](#cite_note-15)

## Services

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Services")]

Main articles: [Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Elastic_Compute_Cloud "Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud") and [Amazon S3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_S3 "Amazon S3")

As of 2025[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit) AWS comprises over 200[[14]](#cite_note-techradar-16) products and services including [computing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computation "Computation"), [storage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Elastic_File_System "Amazon Elastic File System"), [networking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_network "Computer network"), [database](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Database "Database"), [analytics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Analytics "Analytics"), [application services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Application_service_provider "Application service provider"), [deployment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_deployment "Software deployment"), [management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Systems_management "Systems management"), [machine learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning"),[[15]](#cite_note-17) [mobile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mobile_application_development "Mobile application development"), [developer tools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_tool "Programming tool"), RobOps and tools for the [Internet of Things](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_of_Things "Internet of Things"). The most popular include [Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Elastic_Compute_Cloud "Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud") (EC2), [Amazon Simple Storage Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Simple_Storage_Service "Amazon Simple Storage Service") (Amazon S3), Amazon Connect, and [AWS Lambda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AWS_Lambda "AWS Lambda") (a [serverless function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serverless_computing "Serverless computing") that can perform arbitrary code written in any [language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Programming_language "Programming language") that can be configured to be triggered by hundreds of [events](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Event_(computing) "Event (computing)"), including [HTTP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP "HTTP") calls).[[16]](#cite_note-mostpopularservices-18)

Services expose functionality through APIs for clients to use in their applications. These APIs are accessed over HTTP, using the [REST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/REST "REST") architectural style and [SOAP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SOAP "SOAP") protocol for older APIs and exclusively [JSON](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JSON "JSON") for newer ones. Clients can interact with these APIs in various ways, including from the AWS console (a website), by using [SDKs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_development_kit "Software development kit") written in various languages (such as [Python](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Python_(programming_language) "Python (programming language)"), [Java](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Java_(programming_language) "Java (programming language)"), and [JavaScript](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JavaScript "JavaScript")), or by making direct REST calls.

### Founding (2000–2005)

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Amazon_Web_Services&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Founding (2000–2005)")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/5/5d/Amazon.com_web_services_2002.jpg/250px-Amazon.com_web_services_2002.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Amazon.com_web_services_2002.jpg)

Early AWS "building blocks" logo

The genesis of AWS came in the early 2000s. After building *Merchant.com*, Amazon's e-commerce-as-a-service platform that offers third-party retailers a way to build their own web-stores, Amazon pursued [service-oriented architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Service-oriented_architecture "Service-oriented architecture") as a means to scale its engineering operations,[[17]](#cite_note-horsemouth-19)[[18]](#cite_note-foraws-20)[[19]](#cite_note-tcaws-21)[[20]](#cite_note-crnaws-22)[[21]](#cite_note-hilabs-23)[[22]](#cite_note-vdynamo-24)[[23]](#cite_note-vogels-25) led by then [CTO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chief_technology_officer "Chief technology officer") Allan Vermeulen.[[24]](#cite_note-brad-26)

Around the same time frame, Amazon was frustrated with the speed of its software engineering, and sought to implement various recommendations put forth by Matt Round, an engineering leader at the time, including maximization of autonomy for engineering teams, adoption of [REST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Representational_state_transfer "Representational state transfer"), standardization of infrastructure, removal of gate-keeping decision-makers (bureaucracy), and [continuous deployment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Continuous_deployment "Continuous deployment"). He also called for increasing the percentage of the time engineers spent building the software rather than doing other tasks.[[25]](#cite_note-velocity-27) Amazon created "a shared [IT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_Technology "Information Technology") platform" so its engineering organizations, which were spending 70% of their time on "undifferentiated heavy-lifting" such as IT and infrastructure problems, could focus on customer-facing innovation instead.[[26]](#cite_note-28)[[27]](#cite_note-aselip-29) Besides, in dealing with unusual peak traffic patterns, especially during [the holiday season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics_of_Christmas "Economics of Christmas"), by migrating services to commodity Linux hardware and relying on [open source software](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_source_software "Open source software"), Amazon's Infrastructure team, led by Tom Killalea,[[28]](#cite_note-tompeak-30) Amazon's first [CISO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CISO "CISO"),[[29]](#cite_note-31) had already run its data centers and associated services in a "fast, reliable, cheap" way.[[28]](#cite_note-tompeak-30)

In July 2002 Amazon.com Web Services, managed by Colin Bryar,[[30]](#cite_note-32) launched its first [web services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Web_service "Web service"), opening up the Amazon.com platform to all developers.[[31]](#cite_note-33) Over one hundred applications were built on top of it by 2004.[[32]](#cite_note-tomlinux-34) This unexpected developer interest took Amazon by surprise and convinced them that developers were "hungry for more".[[27]](#cite_note-aselip-29)

By the summer of 2003, [Andy Jassy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Jassy "Andy Jassy") had taken over Bryar's portfolio[[33]](#cite_note-working-35) at [Rick Dalzell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Dalzell "Rick Dalzell")'s behest, after Vermeulen, who was Bezos' first pick, declined the offer.[[24]](#cite_note-brad-26) Jassy subsequently mapped out the vision for an "Internet [OS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operating_System "Operating System")"[[17]](#cite_note-horsemouth-19)[[19]](#cite_note-tcaws-21)[[21]](#cite_note-hilabs-23)[[34]](#cite_note-telaws-36) made up of foundational infrastructure primitives that alleviated key impediments to shipping software applications faster.[[17]](#cite_note-horsemouth-19)[[18]](#cite_note-foraws-20)[[19]](#cite_note-tcaws-21)[[21]](#cite_note-hilabs-23)[[23]](#cite_note-vogels-25) By fall 2003,[[17]](#cite_note-horsemouth-19)[[19]](#cite_note-tcaws-21) [databases](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Databases "Databases"), [storage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cloud_storage "Cloud storage"), and [compute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compute "Compute") were identified as the first set of infrastructure pieces that Amazon should launch.[[17]](#cite_note-horsemouth-19)[[19]](#cite_note-tcaws-21)[[27]](#cite_note-aselip-29)

Jeff Barr, an early AWS employee, credits himself, Vermeulen, Jassy, Bezos, and a few others for coming up with the idea that would evolve into [EC2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_EC2 "Amazon EC2"), [S3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_S3 "Amazon S3"), and [RDS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_RDS "Amazon RDS");[[35]](#cite_note-37) Jassy recalls the idea was the result of brainstorming for about a week with "ten of the best [technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_engineering "Software engineering") minds and ten of the best [product management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_management "Product management") minds" on about ten different Internet applications and the most primitive building blocks required to build them.[[21]](#cite_note-hilabs-23) [Werner Vogels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Werner_Vogels "Werner Vogels") cites Amazon's desire to make the process of "invent, launch, reinvent, relaunch, start over, rinse, repeat" as fast as it could was leading them to break down [organizational structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_company "Big company") with "two-pizza teams"[[c]](#cite_note-39) and [application structures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Software_architecture "Software architecture") with [distributed systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_computing "Distributed computing");[[d]](#cite_note-40) and that these changes ultimately paved way for the formation of AWS[[23]](#cite_note-vogels-25) and its mission "to expose all of the atomic-level pieces of the Amazon.com platform".[[37]](#cite_note-41) According to [Brewster Kahle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brewster_Kahle "Brewster Kahle"), co-founder of [Alexa Internet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexa_Internet "Alexa Internet"), which was acquired by Amazon in 1999, his start-up's compute infrastructure helped Amazon solve its [big data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_data "Big data") problems and later informed the innovations that underpinned AWS.[[38]](#cite_note-42)

Jassy assembled a founding team of 57 employees from a mix of engineering and business backgrounds to kick-start these initiatives,[[21]](#cite_note-hilabs-23)[[20]](#cite_note-crnaws-22) with a majority of the hires coming from outside the company.[[21]](#cite_note-hilabs-23) They included Jeff Lawson, the [Twilio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twilio "Twilio") CEO;[[39]](#cite_note-43) Adam Selipsky, the [Tableau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tableau_Inc "Tableau Inc") CEO;[[40]](#cite_note-44)[[41]](#cite_note-45) and Mikhail Seregine,[[42]](#cite_note-46) a co-founder at [Outschool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outschool "Outschool").

In late 2003, the concept for compute,[[e]](#cite_note-48) which would later launch as [EC2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_EC2 "Amazon EC2"), was reformulated when Chris Pinkham and Benjamin Black presented a paper internally describing a vision for Amazon's retail computing infrastructure that was completely standardized, completely automated, and would rely extensively on web services for services such as storage and would draw on internal work already underway. Near the end of their paper, they mentioned the possibility of selling access to virtual servers as a service, proposing the company could generate revenue from the new infrastructure investment.[[44]](#cite_note-PinkhamBlack2003Paper-49)[*[unreliable source?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources")*] Thereafter Pinkham, [Willem van Biljon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willem_van_Biljon "Willem van Biljon"), and lead developer Christopher Brown developed the Amazon EC2 service, with a team in [Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town "Cape Town"), South Africa.[[45]](#cite_note-50)

In October 2004, Amazon released Alexa Web Information Service (AWIS) as beta.[[46]](#cite_note-51) In November 2004, AWS launched its first [infrastructure service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IaaS "IaaS"), as beta: [Simple Queue Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Simple_Queue_Service "Amazon Simple Queue Service") (SQS).[[47]](#cite_note-52)[[48]](#cite_note-53)[[49]](#cite_note-54), and officially launched in July 2006.[[50]](#cite_note-55)[[51]](#cite_note-auto2-56)
